utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. I was informed that Mr. Stewart will not be with us this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour. He will be arriving after the first break, but he's attending to some other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Karagiannakis, you may proceed with your examination-in-chief, but not after I have reminded you, Witness 224, that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've made yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: I'd just like to recap where we left your testimony yesterday and I'll continue with some questions after that. You were telling us about the 4th of May. You'd been taken to Luka. You were in an office. A policeman had told you that you were to be interrogated. Now, what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were offered a drink, a cup of coffee, fruit juice. This person tried to convince us that it would be just a formal interrogation, that there was no reason for us to worry about anything. He tried to relax us. However, after only a little while a man stormed in. He was angry. He grabbed a policeman who was sitting there. He pushed him out of the office, physically pushed him out. The policeman was trying to fight him. He tried to explain that he was in charge of us and that he should be in the office, but the man didn't care. He fired a few shots in the air and then returned to the office on his own without the policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Had you seen that man before?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: What was that man wearing?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Can you describe the military uniform?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was like a camouflage uniform with leaves of olive green colour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Did you subsequently learn who that man was?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And who was he?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ranko Cesic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: All right. What did Ranko Cesic do?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he returned into the office, he started shouting so much that the whole room was shaking. The blood vessels in his neck were tense. He was spitting with anger. He started cursing our balija mothers, us balijas. And then he first --

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: If I can just stop you there. What does "balija" mean?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the first time I ever heard this word and I ever learned of this name balija. In my view, balija is probably an ugly name for a Muslim -- for the Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: All right. What else did he say?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He cursed us. He said he hated all Muslims. His every word was a swear word. He grabbed the doctor who was standing in front of him and then started beating him on his head first with a boxer and then he hit him with a rifle butt. The whole room was resounding. The man was screaming. He fell down on the ground and then he started stomping all over him with his boots. He was kicking him. He was hitting him. And then the doctor stopped moving. And then he grabbed Mustafa and Rasko. He then kicked and hit the two of them. He was cursing all this time. He was so beside himself that he was beating them until the moment they fell to the ground. He broke out in sweat. He was tired from all this beating. And then he ordered the two people who fell down to stand up. The two -- the people stood up. They were afraid. This is the kind of terror I had never seen before. This was us facing this terror that paralysed all of us. People slowly got on their feet. Some would stumble and fall down. Then he would kick them again. Eventually, all the people stood up and were standing on their feet. Then he ordered one of our employees who was the strongest of all of us, he ordered him to hit me with a boxer. The man --

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Can I just stop you there? When you say "boxer," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a fist which looks like a boxer's fist. And he told him to hit me with his fist and if he didn't hit me hard enough he would hit him. So this man didn't think twice. He hit me with this boxer fist. I fell behind a desk that was behind me. I fell between two chairs, or two armchairs. I don't know what those were. And that's how I remained lying down. He ordered me to stand up, ordered me to move forward, and again, three or four times, he ordered the same man to hit me with his fist and every time I would fell behind the desk. And then he ordered everybody to hit each other with their fists in the head, and people were beating each other. They were wet. They were bloodstained but they had to do it. They had to beat each other to give him the time to rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: When you say the people were hitting each other, which people do you mean?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The people who had been brought from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: After some time did anybody else come into the office?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cesic ran out from the room and brought a man. We heard a shot from -- coming from the outside. This man that he brought in was terrified. He was bloodstained. He was shaking. He was begging and crying. And as he was bringing this man in, he was hitting him with his rifle butt, and he was kicking him. Those were terrible scenes. The beg -- the man was begging him to stop beating him. He said he would do anything he wanted him to do, but this Cesic continued like a maniac. And the man stopped crying. I believe that he had broken his -- every bone in his body. The beating was terrible. It was awful. It was unbearable.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Take your time, madam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam, if you -- if you would prefer to have a short break if you feel that your emotions are such that you could not continue, please indicate so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just give me a moment to calm down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be a good idea to take a five-minute break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would it be a good idea, Witness 224, that we have a short break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Five minutes. If you can give me just to go out, wash my face, I'll be okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For going out we have to leave the curtains down. We will adjourn for five minutes. --- Break taken at 2.31 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber intends to allow the witness to be accompanied by a person of the victims and witness section. If there is any observation to be made for the parties, I'd like to know. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: There's no observation to be made, Your Honour, from the Defence perspective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could the witness please be escorted in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 224, the Chamber understands that giving testimony may well be very emotional an experience for you. The Chamber understands that, and you don't have to be ashamed of it. And if you need any extra time, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. All my life dedicated to working and helping for people, and for the first time I met -- I faced something that was inconceivable, so I experienced a terrible shock, and I still feel the pain. It was really a painful experience. And now having to go through this just revives this pain. But I still want to continue with this testimony. I want to tell the truth and nothing but the truth. I want to inform you about the truth. I want the criminals to be punished. I want the crime to be punished. That's my own goal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 224, this Chamber is trying to find the truth and has understanding for your emotions. Ms. Karagiannakis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: After the end of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: After the end of that beating -- or those beatings, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He pushed all of us outside. He simply just pushed us outside. He was behind us pushing us, and I could just feel that I was being pushed in that direction. I looked to the side. There was a number of soldiers there. They continued to push us towards the hangar, towards the wall near the door. I looked to the side. There was some people next to me, but at that point I couldn't see all of them. I was pushed up to the hangar wall, and I was the first next to the door along that wall.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: You said there was some people at the hangar door. Do you remember how many?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were ordered to lean against the wall, pushed off with our legs. I raised my head a little bit, and I could see that there was a column back there. I couldn't see the end of it. The people who were standing along the wall with their hands on the wall and with their faces towards the wall.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Do you remember how many people there were?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a very long column numbering possibly about 50 people. From what I saw as I was coming to the place, and then when I looked from the side, I could see this column, very long column, and I couldn't see the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: What were the people in the column wearing?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were civilians. Their clothes were civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Behind me the soldiers were talking. I didn't hear what they were saying. I heard them say that we should line up, and there was an order to fire. At that point, I don't know why I turned towards the line. I turned to my side, and that's when I saw that it was a column of approximately 50 people. As I say, I don't know why I turned around. At that moment, somebody spoke up. "What are you doing? Why are you turning around?" And I didn't know that I was being addressed until I could sense somebody come up to me and pull me by my hand out of that line, and then they pulled me past those soldiers. This person was walking alongside me holding my hand. And as I was passing by the soldiers, I heard the order to fire, and I could hear a terrible blast. I could hear the firing of a large number of rifles, and you could smell the gunpowder in the air, and it was irritating my eyes and my face. This smell of gunpowder and the smoke were very irritating for the eyes. I continued to walk. I didn't dare turn around because this soldier was still holding my hand. So I didn't turn around, but subconsciously I was expecting -- even though I couldn't turn around, I wanted to hear what was happening behind me. Was it really possible that those people were killed? I just wanted to at least hear the falling bodies, the sound of the bodies that were falling. And I did hear that. I heard the bodies as they fell, and I could hear the sounds, the sighs, moans of people. As the people were falling, they were making these sounds, and you could hear these dull thuds of those 50 bodies falling to the cement. I was then brought back to the same room where I was before. Once I was brought into the room, I didn't hear the soldier. I didn't see the soldier any more. And then I heard the sound of Branko Cesic's voice. He was shouting and pushing me inside that room. I found myself alone with him in that room. He placed a chair next to the wall, and he ordered me to sit down. He placed a second chair in front of me. He turned his automatic rifle towards me. It was almost pointing at me, and he fired. And I could smell the gunpowder and the smoke, and I could see the bullet entering the wall. And he said that in order -- he wanted to just question me a little bit, play around with my nerves. He asked me about my work, what was I doing, how was he killing their Serb children. I was dumbfounded. I didn't know where he got the idea to say such things to me. Then he asked about my husband. He asked a lot about my husband. He asked me about my work. He said, "I just want to play around with you a little bit to decide what to do with you." Then he ordered me -- I don't know how long this took. It seemed to last an eternity for me. Each minute seemed like a year. It was terrible to go through something like that. Then he pulled me out and made me leave. I was walking in front of him, and then there was a vehicle, a van or some kind of vehicle which was outside. He made me go in and sit to the seat next to the driver's seat, the front passenger's seat. He sat down in the driver's seat and the vehicle set off. I could sense two German shepherds, two very large dogs that were behind me, and I could feel their breath. They were breathing behind me. They were close to me, so I could just sense their saliva falling onto my shoulders. Then we turned around. We came up to the hangar entrance. He ordered the guards to open the hangar, which is what they did, and then he turned to the right. He went towards the hangar. It was terrible for me. At the same time, I was ashamed, and I was afraid. Everything was mixed up together. I didn't know where to look, because I was so afraid, and because of the fear, my eyes were just gazing around the walls. I looked to the side through the window, and I could see that people were lined up with their hands up. They were lined up along the wall around the hangar. He went around the hangar slowly, and he was listing some things to himself. I don't know what it was. I was disturbed by the growling of the dogs while we were driving around through the hangar. He was going very slowly, and I could see every wall, every side, and I saw a lot of people. I estimate that there were perhaps about 100 people there who were civilians. This is what I was able to estimate in spite of my fear. They were wearing different civilian clothes, jeans, shirts, T-shirts. I am sure, 100 per cent sure that they were all civilians. I don't remember, I didn't see, and I cannot say for certain whether I saw soldiers inside or not. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. A circle was formed. Very soon we were outside. He turned towards the gate going out of Luka. They opened the gate very quickly. The guards opened it very quickly because they probably knew him well. He drove straight towards the bridge. It was already dark. It was the first time that I noticed it was already dark. We were on the street going towards the bridge. He stopped the car, and then he told me that he had to play with me, that he made the decision what he was going to do with me and that the first time -- that the first thing he wanted to do was to rape me. Then he took a knife out. He had the knife in his boot, a very large knife with a serrated edge. He placed it on my neck. The dogs heads were just above me. I was very afraid. I grabbed the car door, the door handle, with one hand. With my other hand, he just simply took my other hand and pulled it towards him, and then he said -- he pulled my hand, and then he started to lift my skirt. He started to undress me. He opened up his trousers, and at that point I was petrified. He said that I shouldn't move and that he would use the knife if I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Witness, can you just in one sentence describe what happened next? No need for details.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He raped me. And while he was raping me, he said that it was a pleasure to have one more balija woman to rape, something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: What happened after he finished raping you?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As he was zipping himself up, he said, "We're going to a different area now." He said we would go to the bridge where he would cut my throat and throw me into the river. As he said that, some lights appeared. They were from -- came from the back, and they lit up the front part. Somebody stopped in their vehicle behind us. A man came out. I didn't know who he was. He came out, and he said, "Ranko, come out." Ranko didn't respond immediately. He just looked through the window. Then he told me, "Please, you have to come out. We have to talk." So that man was trying to get him to come out of the car so that they could talk. Ranko went out of the car. They began to talk normally, then a louder conversation ensued. It was more like an argument. Then the argument became even louder, and then I heard this other man telling him, "Why did you take an inmate out without permission?" He was berating him. He was not allowed to do that. He needed to have permission. So this was the gist of that conversation. Then the person who was the driver actually told this other person to come out, and then all three of them stood there and talked. There was a little bit of pushing, and the argument was a little bit heated. However, the man who was driving left his companion to discuss things with Ranko, and in the conversation they mentioned Ranko Cesic. And this is the first time that I found out his name. The driver then came around to my side. He opened the door and asked me nicely -- first he introduced himself. He said, "Madam, my name is Dragan. Please don't be afraid. Please come into my car. Nothing will happen to you. I'm going to take you." So I went into his car. The man sat down. Dragan sat down, and he drove straight towards the SUP. So those two men, the driver -- the co-driver and Ranko Cesic left -- were left behind in that place where we were while the two of us, Dragan and I, found ourselves in front of the SUP. He stopped in front of the SUP. He parked the car. There were a lot of soldiers in front of the SUP, in military uniform. They were all kinds of uniforms. They were moving around. They were not standing still. They were going in one direction and coming back. That was large number of soldiers. Perhaps about 50 of them were there. However, Dragan got out of the car and crossed over to my side, and, holding my hand, he passed and went up the stairs, and he escorted me to the right side, to an office. He took me into the office. We were alone. Dragan tried to calm me down a little bit, to tell me that I was in safe hands, that nothing will happen, and what he wanted to do was to just do a formal interrogation and that I should not be afraid. He even asked somebody to bring me some coffee. He offered me a cigarette so that I could calm down. This took some time, because I was shaking all over. It took me a while to calm down so that he could ask questions and that I could answer his questions. After about perhaps half an hour or so I calmed down, and he started to question me very kindly about my family. I answered what I could, what I knew of my family, where they were, where they were living. I gave him the answers, and then he said that the main interrogation should be conducted by Dragan Veselic, the chief of the SUP, and that they were waiting for him to be free. And we waited for a little bit for him to come to us. Not a long time afterwards, Dragan took me up to the third floor. He was walking alongside of me. He took me to the third floor where there was a kind of conference room. There was a round table there with chairs, and there were about four soldiers inside this room. One was next to the door, two were at the end of the room, and one of them was walking between the table and the windows. So as I came in, again they brought a chair next to the door for me to sit down. The man who was walking around sat down opposite me. He asked me, "Look at me carefully. Do you know me?" He repeat this had a couple of times. "Look at me carefully." The man was shaven with short hair, wearing soldier's clothing. I looked at him for a while and I said that I didn't know him. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then he started to interrogate me. He asked me about my family. Mostly he asked about my friends, our common friends with whom we socialised before the war. These friends with whom I had contacts with were people from mixed marriages. They were of all religions, all mixed up. However, I told him I didn't know where those people were. And I really didn't know where they were. From the beginning, I was in the hospital, I didn't know what was going on outside. I didn't know what was going on in town. Then he began to count back. He gave me an ultimatum. He said I had one minute to respond or he would kill me, and I said, "Sir, you can kill me, but I cannot give you answers to questions to which I don't know the answers," and this is how I finished with my answers. After that, there was a more strict conversation. The tone changed. After a while it became a little bit more mild. He asked me, actually, what I wanted to do now, and I said that I would like to go back to my work where I was and from where I was taken away. And then he said, "Very well." He told the others --

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Can I just stop you there and ask you, the Dragan Veselic that you knew before the war, what did he look like?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He had a moustache and a beard, and he had long, slightly curly hair. He was tall, thin, brown-eyed. I even know that he was a vegetarian, because we socialised. That's why he was very skinny. He was tall. I know his face very well from before the war. So that throughout all the changes -- and the uniform and the shaved face and the shaved moustache, his face was smooth, shaved smoothly, and his hair was cut short -- so because of that, all of those changes, I didn't recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: All right. Now, were you subsequently taken back to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, escorted by two soldiers. They brought me to the car --

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And did you stay at the hospital during that next day?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was already when I left the SUP. It was almost dawn, and I think I even asked one of the soldiers what time it was, and they said it was about 4.00 a.m. So it was already almost dawn. They Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. escorted me to the hospital. There was no conversation between us. They brought me to the door, and they left me there, and I went inside, into the hospital to my workplace. When I came to my workplace, one of my colleagues was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Can I stop you there. Did you stay at the hospital for the whole duration of -- for most of that day?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes. And were you at any stage taken out of the hospital again?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in the afternoon when Dragan Zivkovic came to my workplace and called me again. He said that-and-that person, he said, "Who is so-and-so?" And I said that was me. I thought the first time that I was brought back the interrogations would be over and that I was finished with that, but when he came to get me for the second time and when I was taken away again to the same place, I understood that this is actually just the beginning of everything that was happening. I left with him. We went downstairs. We went to the -- a little bit towards the dialysis department in that corridor. We stopped there. We waited. There were another two nurses there, and then again I saw the doctor, the same doctor that was taken away together with me that first evening. And I told him through the -- they told us that we should enter the doors of the dialysis and go towards them. And there was one soldier there. So we went after them. We followed them. As we were escorted and we were walking past, for the first time I saw a large quantity of weapons in the rooms where the dialysis ward was, and also towards the entrance. At the entrance itself, I could see that the hospital courtyard was absolutely filled with weapons. You couldn't see the courtyard for the weapons. They told us to sit in the back seat of a vehicle. I remember is that Kosta was the driver, because I remember, I know that Kosta is the husband of one of our nurses who used to work in the -- in one of the hospital wards. There was also Dragan Zivkovic. He was the husband of one of the nurses who worked in the dialysis section. So I knew them as the husbands of these nurses who worked with us. And then there was the following conversation: I remember now that I saw the staff in the corridors who had not turned up for their shifts. They were all of Serb ethnicity. I could see in the corridors nurses who were supposed to report to work but they did not come. They were in ironed uniforms. They looked like models. They wore make-up. They were very groomed. They were walking up and down the corridors, and that was the first time that they had reported to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Were you taken at that stage back to Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They drove us through the town, and then Kosta, the husband of one of our colleagues, said that he was sorry, that he didn't like what was going on. He wasn't in favour of that but that he had to do his duty and that he was just the driver and that he did not want to get involved that. So it was as if he was trying to justify himself through that conversation, and while doing that, he brought us to the same place, back to the Luka, back to the same room.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And who was in the room when you entered?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told to enter the room. We entered. In a corner, there were people in light blue police uniforms. There was a young man sitting in that corner, very young, maybe around 25, and another person, a girl, a very young girl. They were sitting in a corner, and to the side there were three or four policemen standing next to them. They brought us in, and they put us in front of Goran Jelisic's desk. We were standing in front of his desk. Goran Jelisic introduced himself to us. He said, "I'm Goran Jelisic, also known as Serbian Adolf Hitler. My duty is -- and I've been given the green light, my hands are free to do whatever I want because Muslims have a lot of children -- my duty is to eradicate the Muslim people. My duty is to hate Muslims, to hate balijas." He says he couldn't support balijas, that he was irritated by balijas. Goran Jelisic such started in a somewhat milder tone, but as he went on speaking, he started looking more and more irritated. He was yelling and shouting while he was delivering his words. He said a lot of things. I can't repeat everything. I can't remember everything. I can remember just some of it. In any case, it all boiled down to the hatred of Muslims and that his job was to eradicate Muslims because there were too many of them. He also said, "Don't count on the Red Cross. Don't count on international organisations. They were not help you." He said that he was our god and our lord, and everything that was to happen would be his decision. He said, "Abandon all hope, because your destiny is in my hands." As he said that, for the first time I realised what he was saying was the truth, that he had the green light to do whatever he wanted to do, because the way he spoke, he was so assured of himself that I felt convinced that what he was saying was the truth. And then I realised that the circle was full, that it was a death circle and that this would be our end, the end of us. He ordered us -- things. He wanted to prove his power and his influence. He ordered a prisoner to be brought from the hangar. They brought him. He ordered us to look in front of us. They ordered a man to be brought in. The man was indeed brought in. He was pushed into the room. They pushed him into the middle of the room. The room was very small, three by four metres big. Then he ordered -- ordered other policemen to stand up and to encircle this man. He stood up himself. They were shouting. They were shouting insults. And although my eyes were cast down, I still wanted to see what was going on. They were beating him so heavily. Those kicks were so forceful. The man was screaming and yelling. I could see his legs. And he had a pair of trainers on his feet. He was a civilian. They were beating him with animal fierceness. They were bloodthirsty, and one could hear screams of this poor man. I just can't repeat that. I'm sure that something -- at that moment something must have happened to me because of all the fear that I felt at that time. I lack words to explain how I felt at that moment, and I am ashamed, but I have to say that I peed in my pants out of fear. I'm ashamed to admit that. They were beating this man until he fell to the floor, and then they stomped all over him. They hit him with rifle butts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And no one could no longer hear him screaming or shouting or begging for mercy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Witness, when this beating was over, what happened? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They pulled the victim outside. He ordered him to pull the victim outside. The rest of us stayed in the room. And after all that, he told us, "This is just an example of what could happen to you." And then they ordered them to take us to the room where we would be accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: You were taken to that room?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a small office across from the hangar door. It was a small room. We could only sit. There was no room for us to stretch our bodies. We gathered in that room. We stayed there. We tried to calm down a little, to come to our senses. We were hoping that this was the end of the ordeal. However --

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Were you in the room with two females and a male?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And were those people Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They -- those people had been brought from the hospital. The four of us who were brought from the hospital were put into that same room. They put us in that one room.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you were taken out of that room?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you when it happened. In any case, it was not long Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. before the door was opened. A solder walked into the room. He kicked me with his boot as I was sitting closest to the door. He was carrying a huge big torchlight. I had never seen such a big torch lamp before. He point it had in my eyes. He held it like that for a while and he said, "Follow me." I was blinded by the light. I was touching the walls in order to see where I was going. I was walking in front of him. He was pushing me from the back, and then he returned me to the room where Goran Jelisic was, to that same room. I was taken into that room again. I was standing in front of Goran Jelisic. This time I was on my own. The three others had stayed behind. Then he first told me that he hated Muslim women, that Muslim women are dirty, that he didn't want to touch a Muslim woman. He insulted me some more, and then he ordered the others to bring in another nurse. He repeated the same words when that nurse was brought in. He was saying a lot of things about women, but what I can remember is that he said that he hated all Muslim women. And then the third nurse was brought in and the doctor. We were brought in individually, one by one. Again we experienced the same kind of swearing. He called us balijas. He said he would show us another example. He ordered them to bring another person. They brought this other person. They put him in the middle of the room, and again he ordered the others to make a circle around that -- that person, and the same scene repeated: Screams, beatings, yelling, crying for help.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: All right. Can I stop you there, Witness, please. After that second beating, were you then taken back to the room where you had come from?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They brought me back to that same room.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And did you stay there for some time?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did not even have enough time to calm down. It was so hard. We were in such a state of shock it was very difficult to calm down. We tried to comfort each other as much as we could. And again after a little while, a soldier came, again kicked me with his boot, again directed the torchlight into my eyes and ordered me to go out. As I stepped out, again I tried to find my bearings. I thought that I was being taken to the same thing again, to experience another beating. However, at one moment I was pulled to a different side, to another room. All of a sudden I found myself in a different room where I saw another desk. There was a lamp on that desk. The room was somewhat dark, and I saw a woman lying down on the floor undressed, and there was a soldier above her buttoning himself up, and there were two other soldiers standing next to her. I just had a glimpse of that scene. I was then pushed behind the desk. As I was pushed, I fell behind the desk, and two of the soldiers whom I couldn't see properly at that time, I was fighting them. I was physically fighting them. I was trying to push them away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Witness, can I stop you there. Were you raped in that room by two people?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name of those two people, the names of those two people?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zuco, Makivija Stojanovic, and the third person whose turn it was to rape me, somebody entered and shouted, "Action, action, quickly." They had to leave quickly. They buttoned themselves up very quickly, and I remained lying on the ground exhausted, powerless. Then as I was able to walk, I dragged myself across the corridor to my room. When I got to my room -- but before I say that, I apologise. I forgot to say while this was happening, I heard a woman's screams. I could hear a woman screaming, and when I returned to my room, I saw Dr. Mufti was crying like a little child. The three of us, the three nurses, we were all crying. He wanted to comfort us. He apologised for not being able to help us. He felt really bad. He didn't know what was going on. And in that conversation, he tried to comfort us. He took the shirt off his face -- his body. There were bruises all over his body. His body was more black and blue than of normal colour. He had been heavily beaten, and whenever he moved, his whole body hurt. Then he told us that on the first night when we were taken away, that Ranko Cesic of killed another man and that he had seen it with his own two eyes. He had seen when this happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Now, you remained in that room, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We remained until the following morning. We couldn't sleep. There was not enough room. The hangar door opened. They started taking people out of the hangar. They would line them in three or four rows. I could hear Jelisic's voice. He was loud. He was shouting. He would order them to sing Serbian songs. He would run through the lines of people with his pistol. He was shouting. He wanted to see whether every single individual was singing, singing properly. He was waving his arms. He was probably firing his pistol. I cannot confirm that he killed anybody because I couldn't see that. There was a guard watching us all the time. But from time to time, we could throw a glance. He would then return to the hangar. More soldiers would come to the hangar. There was more beatings, shouts, crying, cries for help. Then they would take people in front of the hangar. And this all lasted all night. We could not sleep. It would continue almost up to the dawn.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Did this continue -- did these types of beatings continue in the evenings that you were detained at Luka?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Can you please describe for us what your -- apart from those nights where beatings occurred, what your daily routine would be.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first thing that happened in the morning was they would order us to go and clean their toilets and the offices. We would clean blood, bottles, ashtrays full of cigarette butts. They would order us to clean all that. That was our first task in the morning. Once we completed that, they would order us to go to a small kitchen. The kitchen was across the hall from our room. And then we would be ordered to serve food to the troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: You said you used to clean offices. Now, did you ever notice anything in particular when you were cleaning offices?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every day we worked like that. My colleague and I were cleaning. She would take out bottles, and I would dust or clean the blood. I would clean the desk, and on one occasion when I was dusting the desk I saw four or five pieces of paper. I never paid too much attention to these papers until one time when I saw that the title "The List of People to be Executed." When I saw this title, I just couldn't help myself. I had to look. I was very, very frightened, but I just couldn't help myself. I wanted to have a look at that paper. I had the best look at the first paper. I spent somewhat less time on the second paper. However, having read the first paper, I could conclude that this was a list of people, some of them Croats but most of them Muslims. I can't remember any name. I did it in a haste. I really can't remember, but judging by the names, I knew some of these people. I knew that these people were either prominent, educated, or well-off people. This is what I could conclude based on that first paper. About 50 people were on that list altogether. I didn't want to dust the desk on that day. I was afraid that somebody might suspect that I had read the paper. I didn't want anybody to suspect that I had been in the position to read the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Were the people on the list men or women, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly men. I don't remember having seen any female names on that list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Now, after that time, did you become very sick for two or three days and have to remain in the room where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had problems with my urinary organs. I had a high temperature. I suffered a lot of pain. I couldn't move for two days. I can't remember what was happening with me. I believe I was either delirious or in a coma. I didn't know what was going on around me. I was just not there for two days.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And after that time were you raped on a continuous basis by soldiers at Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A colleague of mine, a nurse, obtained some drugs which she gave to me. I can't remember much about that time. I felt somewhat better on the third day. I came to, but I only know that I had -- that my hair had turned grey overnight. I lost a lot of weight. And the same things repeated after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And were you -- up raped again by Makivija Stojanovic, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One afternoon I was ordered to go to the office next door --

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: It's just sufficient to say yes or no. You don't need to go into detail.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Now, after you recovered from your illness, you continued cleaning, isn't you?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was terrible. They forced us to clean their toilets with our bare hands, and the only thing that they gave us was a stick or a broom. It was terrible. It was disgusting, but they forced us to clean their toilets with our bare hands. Monika was in charge of that. She was the one who supervised our work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever have to have occasion to leave Luka through this period?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were done with distributing food to the soldiers, a car would come with two soldiers in it, and we were told to go to the town to clean houses for Serbian families who were supposed to return. There were usually two soldiers, and there was my colleague and I. It would happen in the afternoon. We would go to these private houses. There was a lot of shattered glasses, and we had to tidy those houses so that the families could move into those houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: What sort of houses were they?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognised the houses. I recognised the furniture in them. I also could tell by the pictures on the walls that those were Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Did the soldiers say anything while you were cleaning these Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They told us that we were supposed to clean because it belonged to them. They said that they were rich and that every Serbian family could have as many as ten houses, but those houses had to be cleaned first. They said that this all belonged to them and that it had to be made nice and tidy for their families.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: After you cleaned houses outside of Luka camp, you subsequently returned to Luka camp, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later in the afternoon, the two -- the same two soldiers would take us back. As we were driving in the car, we had to pass by the bridge, and we had a good view of the Sava River. I saw four or five corpses floating on the water. There may have been even more than that, but I didn't look for long. I could see parts of the trunks and the upper extremities, the arms. Could I see those bodies floating on the water. We were then taken back to Luka and brought into the same room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Karagiannakis, it's close to quarter to four. Would you please find a moment, if this would not be the moment, to have a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: It's a good moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's good moment. May I first ask the witness to be escorted out of the courtroom. Mr. Usher, could you please move the curtains down. Witness, we'll have a break of some 20 minutes. Before we finally will have a break, I would like to ask the attention of the parties, and perhaps specifically of the Defence, on one issue. The witness has used the word "rape" several times. As we all know, rape, apart from the meaning in everyday life, also has a specific meaning. I just would like to inquire from the Defence if it will be contested that when this witness used the word "rape" under the circumstances she described whether it will be contested by the Defence that as a rape apart from the force but as far as the physical acts shall concerned would meet the requirements of the legal concept of rape. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I can indicate that there's no question arising from the Defence in relation to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that prevents us -- makes it not necessary to seek confirmation that the physical acts performed would meet -

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour, and that's why I didn't object to leading through that particular portion because I thought it was important that those matters were not dealt with in any particular detail because it's not a matter, of course, on which there is any contradiction on the part of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's good to know, and that -- we'll then adjourn until five minutes past four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for the record, welcome back in court, Mr. Stewart. Ms. Karagiannakis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'm going to ask you a series of questions. It's sufficient for you to say yes or no at the end of each of the questions, please. Did you -- did the daily and nightly events that you've previously described to the Trial Chamber continue throughout until the 19th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And on that day, did two men arrive in a vehicle at Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th of May, a vehicle arrived and parked between the hangar and our room. The driver was Dragan Veselic, and his co-driver was a person in a military uniform, and he had some rank insignia on his shoulders. As far as I know, that could only be rank insignia. Dragan Veselic began to speak with some of these police officers who were there, so he was just talking to them. And this military officer came out, and one of my colleagues came out and called him into the corridor. At that point, I went out into the corridor, and we asked him to come inside so we could talk to him. The man entered without any problems, and we were standing in the corridor and talking about the situation in the camp. We explained the situation, how horrible things were going on, that this was unbearable, and that we couldn't stand it anymore and that if these really were soldiers, still, we still had some rights. As it was, it was absolutely without any rules. Anybody in the compound could do whatever they wanted. We just requested for some fair behaviour to begin to be applied, because we just asked him, "Please make sure they behave fairly, otherwise, just take your weapons and shoot us. We cannot stand it any more. This is destroying us physically and psychologically." And that man --

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Can I just stop you there. Did you report the rapes you had suffered to this man?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Did you tell him the names of the people who had raped you?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I told him then that -- that there were some people from Serbia. I also mentioned the name of Zuco and Makivija Stojanovic. I remember these two names. I forgot Ranko. I don't know if I did that because I was afraid, but I do know that in the conversation I mentioned these two names. And I said that there were also Serbian soldiers there, and I could tell they were Serbian soldiers because of their accent, the way they talked, but I didn't know their names, so I just told him what I knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And after this time did the crimes that were being committed, the beatings, the murders, and the rapes stop at Luka camp? Yes or no is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation towards us changed completely. He promised that he would post guards in our rooms and that nobody but him was allowed to enter that room and that nobody would be permitted to mistreat us any more. He kept his promise, and from that point on, really, nobody disturbed us any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to ask you a series of questions. Yes or no answer should be sufficient. Were you ever asked to participate in any investigations about the crimes that you had reported to this man?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what --

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Did a policeman ever come to speak to you? After you reported the crimes to this man, did any policeman ever come to speak to you about investigating the crimes that you had reported?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we were in that room and we were just doing regular everyday tasks like cleaning, serving food for their soldiers, I didn't hear Jelisic's voice there any more. Kosta Kostic --

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Perhaps I wasn't clear. Do you know whether Makivija Stojanovic or Zuco were ever punished for what they did to you?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: After the 19th of May, was Jelisic replaced by a man called Kosta?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I could see, Kosta was issuing orders to us to continue with our tasks. He spent most of the time there. I didn't notice Jelisic that much any more. We didn't hear his shouting around any more. On a couple of occasions -- I don't know exactly when, he came in through the gate. I guess he was shouting he wanted to come in. I guess the guards didn't allow him to do that. On another occasion I don't know whether he was allowed to come in or whether he had jumped over the gate, but he was running from the gate to our room, and he threw himself through our windows, and he said, "Just give me one minute. Just let me have one minute to strangle these two snakes." And then this took a while before the guards came. He was going wild. He was holding onto the table. Two or three guards were trying to pull him by his legs to pull him out, but he was resisting them. So in this struggle they managed finally to pull him outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: All right. Now, between the 19th of May and the end of May you were still expected to cook and clean around the camp, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And you were released at the end of May; correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And you were given a pass signed by Kosta that allowed you to travel around the city of Brcko; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And after you were released you were taken to a house next to the SUP in Brcko, and you stayed there.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And you stayed there until the 15th of September when you made contact with the Red Cross and you left Brcko.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm going to ask you, between the time that you were released from Luka camp and the 15th of September, did you notice anything about what had happened to the mosques in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since we were put in this room, we didn't have any food, and hunger made us go out to look for food. We tried, the women, we tried to get together and then four or five of us went in the direction of my house to try to find some food, because food was a problem. We didn't do this every day, but every time when we could, we would go and bring something. Every time hunger made us go out, then we would go and try to bring back something so that we could make it through. Once when we were coming back from our houses, we stopped. We saw that the mosque opposite from the medical centre was in flames. It was still burning, and we stopped because we were not able to pass by because the fire was raging and there were parts of the mosque around on the street. There were some other civilians, passers-by who stood there. Around the mosque there were soldiers, and they were just making comments, and the comments were to the effect that they were glad that the mosque is gone, that it was a thorn in their eye, it was bothering them. They were laughing. They were very happy that it didn't exist any more. And afterwards, when all that rubble was removed, they would plant the grass or they would maybe make a parking lot there. So that was the gist of their comments. In a short while when the flames had subsided a bit, we continued towards the town. We passed by the bijela dzamija, the white mosque. That was also demolished. There was no flame there but you could see the dust rising around the mosque. And that's how we made it home.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: One question in relation to this matter. As you were approaching the mosque near the medical centre, did you hear anything?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was an explosion first.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honours, I'd like to go into closed session for the last part of my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would closed session be needed or would private session do us well?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Private session would be fine. Well, I intend to show some names on the screen and mention them, so if the Sanction screen is not published outside this room, then I think that would be fine, private would be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would mean I would then instruct the technical booth not to show the computer evidence on the composite screen, and could we also check that none of the other screens is such that the public could see it. The only matter is that also for you, the public, perhaps could look over your shoulder. So if you just, for example, for a while use your laptop screen in such a way that the public couldn't see it and then put the other one either off or on the transcript. The laptop wouldn't do? Yes. I'm just looking on whether that could cause any problem at the other side of the -- I can't see from here whether there is anyone in the public gallery on the right-hand side from here. There's no one on this side. Then -- I see people moving to the other side. I'd rather -- I see that they are sitting in the middle. Mr. Usher, would you please keep an eye on that, that no one takes a position in the public gallery from which he could see one of the screens in the courtroom. And the technicians are then instructed not to show the video evidence on the composite picture. I take it that you also read, so we have to go then into private session with these additional measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I find it confirmed on my screen now that we are in open session again. Witness, you'll now be examined by counsel for the Defence. That's Ms. Loukas who will put questions to you. Ms. Loukas, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, good afternoon, Witness 224. I want to assure you that I don't intend to refer to your name or any identifying feature. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, if I say something that you don't understand or that you find yourself needing some time to compose yourself, just let me know. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, I don't have a great many questions to ask you, and hopefully they can be answered fairly easily. For the most part, I will be just asking you to confirm things you've already said on other occasions. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, if we could just briefly go into private session so I can raise a question in relation to -- Your Honour, in relation to the protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Actually -- actually, Your Honour, before we go back into open session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session at this moment, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It's probably a good idea to go back into closed session. There's a further matter I want to raise with Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will now turn into private session. I take it that will do. Yes, that saves us from pulling down the curtains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're in open session again.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Witness 224, as I indicated to you before we went into closed session, I will be very careful to ensure that nothing is said that could in any way reveal your identity, and if there are any questions that I ask that might require that, if you could let me know so that we can immediately go into closed session. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. And as I indicated previously, I don't have many questions, and the -- most of my questions will be just getting you to confirm things that you've said on prior occasions, and I think you understand that.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Witness 224, of course you've given evidence previously in this Tribunal. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course the evidence you gave on that occasion was, of course, subject to a solemn declaration as you are today.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course on that occasion, you gave your evidence, of course, truthfully.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course you gave your evidence accurately.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, at one stage during the proceedings during which you previously gave evidence, do you remember being asked questions by a Judge?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I remember that there were questions by a Judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And what I will do is I will read out to you slowly the question that the Judge asked you and then ask you to confirm whether you remember that question. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, the Judge in question, Judge Riad, said this to you, he said: "Good afternoon. I'm sorry not to call you with your lady's name, just a letter, so that nobody would recognise you." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And he said to you: "I'm trying to understand a little bit more some of your statements. You mentioned that Jelisic declared that he was the man responsible for everything happening." He then said: "I'll try to quote it exactly: That he was the man in charge and that nothing can be done without his permission." The Judge went on to say: "Now, that was his declaration, but on the ground what were the facts? Did the facts corroborate this declaration or was it just somebody boasting about his power and, in fact, it was no so strong?" Now, do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the last part and your question. I could not follow you properly when you were reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: You couldn't follow the Judge's question that I was reading out to you?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I couldn't follow you when you were reading. I couldn't follow you reading from the paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Do you want me to do it more slowly?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll do it more slowly for you. Okay. Do you want me to take it from the top?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not from the very top but when you started reading about Jelisic and his declaration, what he said when you were quoting Jelisic's word. Or maybe, if you find it easier, you may start reading from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I think it's easier if I just read the Judge's question again and I'll do it extra slowly for you, okay?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: "Good afternoon, Witness. I'm sorry not to call you with your lady's name, just a letter, so that nobody would recognise you." Now, you indicated already you remember the Judge saying that. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I'll just read it in little bits. I think that's the easiest way to do it with you. Okay. He then said: "I'm trying to understand a little bit more some of your statements." Do you understand that portion that I've just read to you?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. And then the Judge said: "You mentioned that Jelisic declared that he was the man responsible for everything happening." Now, do you understand that by the of what the Judge said?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: The Judge then said: "I'll try to quote it exactly." And then the Judge went on to quote you. Do you understand that bit?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And this is the bit in quotes that I'm going to read out now. "That he was the man in charge and nothing can be done without his permission." Do you understand that portion?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Then the Judge went on to say to you: "Now, that was his declaration, but on the ground what were the facts?" Do you understand that portion of what he said?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And then he said: "Did the facts corroborate this declaration or was it just somebody boasting about his power and, in fact, it was not so strong?" Now, do you understand at that last bit of the Judge's question?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, what I -- what I will do for you next is actually read out the answer that you gave on that occasion. Do you understand where we're up to now?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your answer was this: "I believe that this was not boasting at all. That was my own perception as well ..." Are you keeping up with your answer so far?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: "... And I tried to remain capable of perception. He enjoyed killing. He enjoyed showing his force, showing that he was god; in other words, that he was our judge, that he decided our fate ..." Are you with me so far on your answer?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: "... And that he had all the strength and all the responsibility for everything that was going on in that camp ..."

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: "... And that he was in charge of everything that was going on in that camp."

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, up until the 19th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, just let me ask you this question: You were asked that particular question, and of course you remember the particular question from the Judge. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And you gave your answer truthfully on that occasion. You've already agreed with that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course you told the truth when you answered the question from the Judge.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So when the Judge asked you the question in relation to Mr. Jelisic, you gave that answer and that answer was the truth.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Witness 224, I'd just now like to take you to the statement that you've given in relation to this matter. I think a copy has been supplied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, may take it that paragraph numbers were added by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We thought it would be easier to refer to the particular paragraphs in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Because it's a rather long statement, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I agree. It's just for our information.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, first, Witness 224, just in relation to that statement, I think that statement was taken over two days. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean over two days?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, the dates of the interview were the 10th and 11th of November, 1998.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And there was, of course, somebody taking notes in relation to what you were saying.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course when you were giving this statement, you realised that the Prosecution wanted your testimony to investigate this matter.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And to find the people responsible.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I think, in fact, this was -- and correct me if I'm wrong -- but your first opportunity to give a statement.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: November 1998?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. Yes, your first opportunity to give a statement to the Prosecution at the ICTY. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course after what had happened to you and -- you knew it was important to tell the truth. That's correct, isn't?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course you gave a detailed statement.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And this statement, of course, was taken over two days and took several hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Do you remember, in fact, how many hours it took?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every day it lasted for seven hours or so.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Right. So the statement probably took around approximately 14 hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course what you did was tell the truth about everything you knew; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course a careful note was being taken of what you said as you said it.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And you had a chance to correct things as they were being written down. That's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the correction. I'm not sure about your question either.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you had a chance to read the entire statement when it was completed.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And before you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, may I ask you to clarify the issue on the front page. I see the languages used. Could you please ask the witness what she read.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: You will notice on the front of the statement, because I understand that -- that you do some -- you do have some understanding of English -- that's correct, isn't?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And on the front of the statement, it indicates 95 per cent English and 5 per cent Bosnian. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So in what language was the interview conducted?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So predominantly it was conducted in English; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And you can read and write English sufficiently?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And that's why you decided to give your interview in English; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was spontaneous.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So you actually spoke in English during the interview?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And when you read the statement, did you read it in English and in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So what basically happened was you gave 95 per cent of your interview in English and -- but when you read your statement at the end, you read the B/C/S version; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course you have good reading and writing skills and speaking skills in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, before you signed your statement, you were asked whether everything was true; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you thinking of English or thinking of both statements? Could you please say that again.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm happy for you to answer in relation to both statements. So when you signed your English statement and when you signed your B/C/S statement, of course obviously you were asked if everything was true; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course you were asked before signing both statements -- that is, the English version and the B/C/S version -- you were asked whether there was anything else you wanted to add. You'd agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course when you signed that statement, it was much closer to the events than we are today. You'd agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: All right. And of course the interviewers were careful with you. You'd agree with that, would you not?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And they allowed your voice, your words, and your story to come out in the statements. That's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, going to your statement, there's just some matters that I'd like to take you to in your statement, and I'd like to take you to paragraph 12 of your statement. Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Paragraph 12 is on page 3 of the statement, and you have that, I think, Witness 224?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just in order to avoid whatever misunderstanding, the paging in the B/C/S version is different from the paging in the English version to the extent that what is page 3, because the front page is not numbered in the B/C/S version where it is in English. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So paragraphs are clearer.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Paragraphs are clearer. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So in any event, we have paragraph 12. Is that correct, Witness?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
