utterances.text: And I just want to confirm with you something you've got in your statement there that wasn't elicited by the Prosecution in your evidence-in-chief and I just wanted to confirm that particular sentence with you. Do you understand? Do you understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. In that -- in paragraph 12, the first sentence states: "The next day, Serb wounded soldiers started to arrive." Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course that was the truth.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, there was another aspect I wanted to refer you to in relation to your statement. So we've just left that issue. There were -- "The next day, Serb wounded soldiers started to arrive." And now I want to take you to paragraph numbered -- okay. Paragraph number 88. Now, Witness, do you have paragraph 88 before you now?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity to read that particular paragraph, paragraph 88?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, that paragraph, of course, refers to just after you'd been ill, and you gave evidence of that earlier today. You recall that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat which period?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, you gave evidence earlier today about the fact that you became very ill and, I think, delirious at one point for two or three days. Do you remember that, giving evidence of that today?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course after you recovered, you gave evidence that you had to attend to cleaning duties. You recall that as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, in that paragraph, paragraph 88, you refer to "Two soldiers escorting us when we left Luka to work." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And you said you did not know these soldiers, and you also said: "Sometimes it was the same soldiers, sometimes it was different soldiers. Do you recall that? That's what's contained in the statement there.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you thinking of the escort to go to work? Perhaps you could allow me read it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I will be more than happy for you to read it. Perhaps it might be good idea to read paragraphs 86, 87, and 88 just to put it in context.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read the passages.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. So now that you've read paragraphs 86, 87, and 88, I think you understand the context in which we're dealing with your evidence at this point; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understood this last part that you are asking for, but I cannot actually determine as a whole what it is that you're seeking.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: All right. All I'm asking for you to confirm for me is that the statement that you made at that paragraph 88, I just want you to confirm that that's your statement and, of course, that's the truth. That's all I'm asking you to do.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So -- and what you've stated there is that you didn't know where those soldiers were from. So you agree with that; is that correct? Those particular soldiers that are dealt with in paragraph 88.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I think you also gave evidence earlier today in relation to a man coming to the camp, and after the visit from this man things changed almost immediately. Do you recall giving that evidence or words to that effect?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So thereafter, the murders, the rapes, and the beatings stopped. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to some other matters contained within your statement that I just want to confirm with you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, if you turn to other matters, I think it's half past five.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, it's half past five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to adjourn until ten to six.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm happy to do that, Your Honour. I'm moving on to a slightly different topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking you just before the weekend do you think that -- and I'm not -- I'm aware that the pace is not just determined by yourself -- do you think that we could finish the cross-examination before the weekend?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: MS. LOUKAS: I must say, Your Honour, as far as I'm concerned, I see no reason not to complete my cross-examination prior to the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Prior to the break? The break is now.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Prior pot break. Prior to the 7.00 break. I think as long as the answers are short, we will definitely be finished by 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All right. We'll adjourn until ten minutes to six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I still think you have the statements in both B/C/S and English before you.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, if you could just go to paragraph 61. Do you have paragraph 61 before you?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I just want to confirm with you a matter that's contained in there in the third sentence. Can you see, referring to Goran Jelisic: "He told us he was in charge of the camp. And anything the soldiers did, they did because he had ordered it." Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, I want to take you to paragraph 108. Do you have that paragraph 108 in front of you in both B/C/S and English?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And in that particular paragraph, you say: "As far as I could see, Goran Jelisic had total power in the camp. The others seemed to obey his orders, and he did what he wanted. He was the person who determined what happened to the detainees. He had the power of life and death, and he liked them to know this. It was part of his fear and power."

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, that, of course, is contained within your statement, Witness.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And it is, of course, the truth.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'd just like to take you to another matter. I think it was, in fact, yesterday that you referred to a term "vojvoda."

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, according to my understanding, that's a term that basically means duke. Does your understanding accord with mine?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, additionally you gave evidence today that at one point the Serb nurses, I think you said -- you said that the, and I'm paraphrasing here, that the Serb nurses had not turned up and that when they did turn up subsequently to work that they were dressed like models, with make-up. Do you remember giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I think you've still got the statement in front of you in both English and B/C/S. If you look at your statement at paragraph 3. Have you got that statement -- that particular paragraph in front of you? So you have that paragraph in front of you now, paragraph 3?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Would you look at the last sentence in that paragraph. What you have there is: "What was unusual was that many nurses did not show up for work that morning." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Of course, you say nothing there about the ethnicity of the nurses. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody asked me.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, if I might just take you back to the questions I asked you earlier in my cross-examination. Before you signed the statement, you were asked if you had anything to add.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And the statement took 14 hours to give.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course you'd gone into a great deal of detail in your statement.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And you wanted to give the truth and the whole truth, leaving nothing out.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But you just failed to mention in your statement the ethnicity of the nurses that didn't turn up; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And if you cast your mind down to -- cast your eyes down to paragraph 5. Do you have that paragraph now?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: You'll notice in the last sentence of that paragraph the statement: "Only about half of the staff that was expected to replace the day shift arrived." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And again, you don't mention anything about ethnicity there; agreed?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to your movements while you were at the camp, I take it you were accompanied around the camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since there was always police or soldiers in the compound, I was always in view of these guards, of the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So you were always in view of the guards and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And when you left the camp to clean houses, you were accompanied by guards?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And at all times when you were in the camp, the guards would not let you out of their sight, would they?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, you've given in evidence that you saw a document on a table; is that correct? I think you gave that evidence today.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Was that document that you say you saw handwritten or typed?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It was handwritten.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, I think you indicated previously that you were never out of the guards' sight; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So I take it you're saying it was only for a matter of seconds that you say you saw this particular document. Is that what you're saying, Witness?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, in relation to that document, it's obvious, is it not, that the document, being handwritten, it would have been a little difficult for you to read that document in a matter of a few seconds. You'd agree with me, with that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The handwriting was very legible. It was almost printed by hand. I wouldn't say a couple of seconds. I managed to just look at this page, just to glance over the names, and the second and third and fourth pages I had less time to look at. I spent less time looking at them.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, I think that you said in your evidence earlier today that you were always in view of the guards; is that correct? Yes?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And that at all times when you were in the camp the guards would not let you out of their sight. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And yet you say that for a matter of seconds you were able to look through a four-page document, is that correct, in handwriting?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since the guard there was standing in front of the door, in front of the building -- actually in front of the entrance to the office, he would never enter after us. He would usually wait in front of the door.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But I thought you said the guards never let you out of your sight -- never let you out of their sight.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but since this was just a room from where -- I did not have anywhere to go. When they were outside, they wouldn't let us out of their sight, but when we entered a room to clean it, they would wait for us in front of the door.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So you're now retracting that answer that you gave previously in evidence, are you, that you were never out of their sight?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No being I'm not retracting. He was at the door.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So you are retracting your answer that you were never out of the guard's sight.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not retracting my answer. He was at the door. He was two metres away from me and there was just this door separating us from him. He could hear every move that we made in that room, and every time we took something out of that room, we had to pass by him.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So you're saying you were out of his sight when you were looking at this list. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So you are retracting the answer that you were always in sight of the guards --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, the matter has been sufficiently dealt with. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would agree it has been sufficiently ventilated.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And, Witness, I believe you initially said it was a matter of seconds that you had to look at the document, but you now you say it was more than a couple of seconds; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The time was short. I can't tell you whether it was two or three seconds. In any case, my colleague was collecting all the bottles, and I went to dust the desk. The guard was standing in front of the room. He wasn't in the room. That's why I could look at the document. Actually, first I saw the title. My one eye was at the entrance. My other eye was on the document. I just had enough time to see the last names of the people on that paper. The desk was in a faraway corner. If the desk was in the line of vision of the guard, somewhere in front of the room, then the guard could have seen me. This is a very small room. In other words, we were still in his sight, but he couldn't see us. The room is small, and the desk is in one of the corners.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: All right. You're saying you were in sight of the guards, but he couldn't see you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that that's actually contradictory?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Loukas. Is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 224, I have a couple of points on which I would like to have clarification. You have told us about the names of some people on a list. Do you still have that list or could it be given to you again. That's the six-page list. Could you please have a look at number 36. You testified that that person -- and you don't have to mention his name at this moment -- you see that, 36? Thirty-six, where the year is indicated as 1932. Yes. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You testified that this person was killed by soldiers. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time? At the first trial?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, just when you answered questions of the Prosecution in private session. Mr. Usher, could you please otherwise show me the list. It's the list. Number 36 appears under ERN number 01038129. It's page 2, indicated page 2. Number 36. You see a name; you don't have to repeat it. And then there's a year, 1932. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You testified today that this person was killed by soldiers. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell me, were you informed about where these soldiers killed this person? I mean, on the street, in a public building, in his house, in a shop? Could you tell us without giving further details?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At home. And his sister witnessed the event. It was in his house, and his sister told me about this event that she had witnessed herself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. Could you then please turn to number 50 on that list. That's the same page, number 50. The fourth from the bottom where a year appears, 1924. You testified that this person was killed at home, but you also testified that his body -- it was unknown as to where his body was. Do I have to understand this as they took this body, dead body from his home and it was never found again? Or could you explain to me, please, the course of events in that respect.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: His family told me about that, his wife and his family. They are still looking for his body, and they don't know where his body is. They want to find his body, but so far his body has not been found and nothing is known of the lot of this person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But did I also understand that he was killed at home?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The -- his family told me that he had been killed at home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then his body was taken by someone? Or was it buried by other -- what happened that they --

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They don't know. They don't know what happened to the body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were they present when he was killed?

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They only heard that from some other people who had seen that. That's how they found out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the family heard that -- from other people that he was killed at home, and they are not aware of where the body was taken.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and they're still trying to find the body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for these answers. Do the questions by the Bench raise any issue that need further clarification?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Witness 224, this concludes your testimony in this Court. The Chamber is aware that it's not easy to be taken back to an episode in your life that certainly has not been easy for you. We are fully aware of that. We appreciate that you came and you answered questions both of the Prosecution and of the Defence and of the Bench, and we wish you a safe trip home.

utterances.speaker: Witness KRAJ-224 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for listening to me and for your participation in all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Usher, could you please, after having pulled the curtains down, escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could deal with the exhibits. Do I understand well, Ms. Loukas, that the Defence tenders into evidence the witness statement, both in English and in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And also the transcript of the testimony on which you put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I think it's probably suitable to accord them a different exhibit number each or one for all, whatever Your Honour prefers in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, it's what the Registry prefers.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's what the registry prefers.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm happy to go with whatever the registry prefers, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We admitted the bundle yesterday. If it's not too cumbersome for the registry, we could continue with that. But if we have to change we'd rather do it now than after a week. Yes. We'd like to split them up in this case because the witness statement should be admitted under seal, whereas the transcript of the testimony could be admitted open. So therefore, perhaps, here is a reason to split them up. Madam Registrar, it would then be for the Defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The transcript will be Defence Exhibit number D3, and the witness statement will be Defence Exhibit D4, under seal, and D4.1 for the B/C/S translation, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have not asked whether there was any objection, but the rule was that you would object whenever the exhibit would be introduced, so I take it there were no objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour. The only comment was going to be about it being under seal, the statement being under seal because it is not redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it was already under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have another question, and that is we could deal with the Prosecution exhibits especially with the bundle in two ways, either to wait until the rest of the documents would be tendered as well and then to admit the whole bundle or now to separate at this very moment the part that has been put to the witness and then wait what will -- what will be presented at a later stage. Any preference?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would seek admission of the first six pages of the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, just the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: That was put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I didn't hear any objections from the Defence on any of the exhibits, therefore, they are admitted into evidence as well. Madam Registrar, would you please guide us through the numbers that have not yet been mentioned and are not yet in the transcript. So all the numbers have been mentioned already before. This is just to clarify that P29 is just the list of six pages and nothing else. Yes. Then we still have more than half an hour, so if the -- well, first -- no. The curtains have to stay down, I think, for your next witness, and I understand that the witness is still available, although it wasn't certain whether we could start with this examination. From the movements on the Prosecution table, I take it that Mr. Hannis, you will examine the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have on my list that it would be Witness 018.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The pseudonym, and that protective measures are in place. And let me just --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Facial distortion and a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that means that the curtains should remain where they are at this moment and that the witness could be escorted into the courtroom. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I wanted to say good afternoon, but it's almost already good evening. We'll wait until the curtains are up. I can just inform you that the protective measures in respect of you are effective. That means that no one can see your face and that we'll not use your name or any identifying data. We will address you as Witness 018. Witness, before giving evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require to you make a solemn declaration. The text of this declaration will be handed to you now, and may I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness 018. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will first be examined by Mr. Hannis, counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Hannis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May the witness please be handed the piece of paper. I don't know if we're giving that a number at this time. And that will be --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number P30, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I noticed, Mr. Hannis, that there's some difference in practice in this Tribunal where in some it's just a name given and others name and date of birth. I've got no idea whether it could create any problem in the future, but please check on your witness list whether it could create any confusion in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness 018, could you please look at that piece of paper before you, and without saying the name, could you please tell us whether that is your name, sir? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May that be returned then and kept under seal. Thank you. And, Your Honour, for the record this is a witness we have offered to introduce his testimony through Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I don't know what procedure the Court would like to follow. It would be my intention merely to proffer him for cross-examination at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He's available for cross-examination. On the other hand, the Chamber, if it would be preferred it by the Prosecution to just ask -- just to introduce it, because this is, of course, a public trial, and it might be very difficult for the world outside to understand anything of it, not having read his 92 bis statement, just perhaps to introduce through four, five, or six very short questions what his statement is about. I think that would be a preferable approach, not that much for the Chamber, but mainly for guaranteeing the public character of this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, we strongly endorse that approach in favour of as much public information as can be given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, Mr. Hannis, of course one of the effects of 92 bis is to save time and, therefore, it should really be limited, but giving as much information as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask a question in that regard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I had proposed the possibility of reading about a page and a half. That's a summary of his statement that was the description of his statement in another case in which he already testified.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: That would be a way. Perhaps in future cases -- I don't not know whether this summary is presented to the Defence first.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is part of his testimony in another case which was given to the Defence, and I can refer them to the page number at which it appears, if that will help.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're not -- in this particular case, we're not troubled by this proposed procedure at all, and normally speaking, we -- we don't require to have yet further paper of this type. If the summary is, as it's clearly going to be, simply an extract of various parts which are in the statement, we're perfectly happy with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course. That what would be my only concern. So if ever such summaries are prepared, I think it would save time if they are given to the other party so that they can verify whether this is really a summary of what is in the statement and not anything else. But I take it that the Defence will take the risk at this time that not --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes indeed, Your Honour. I just have in mind -- of course if any summary is actually prepared, then naturally we would wish to have it. Sometimes we understand that just a very brief oral summary may be given without such a statement being prepared. But we don't have a -- we really don't have a strong objection to that procedure, if that's suitable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's then proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could interpreters have copies of the summaries since the counsel is going to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is contained in the transcript dated 10 December 2003 beginning at page 30215 and going over to 30217.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the Prosecution is invited, first of all, to read slowly if there are no additional copies available, and second of all, to provide additional copies next time if it happens again. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, this defendant's statement -- evidence can be summarised as follows: Prior to the war, the witness was neither a member of the SDS or the SDA and had no political affiliation. Between the night of the 30th of April and the 1st of May, the bridges were blown up in the Brcko area, and various Serb paramilitary groups started to carry out an offensive on Brcko. This witness took refuge in his sister's cellar, and after Brcko was taken by the Serbian forces, those forces came round the various houses. The witness was taken out of the cellar with the others he was hiding with, and they were separated based on ethnicity. This witness and his group were taken to the SUP building where he met a JNA captain who ordered them to be taken to the Posavina Hotel. The man who ordered this separation was known as Dragan. He had an English-sounding accent and was in charge of the Serb forces who had taken him out of the house and to the hotel. At the Posavina Hotel, he saw four dead bodies out of the window, all of which had been piled on top of one another and were wearing civilian clothes. They looked as if they had been recently killed. In the hotel, a man called Goran Jelisic entered the room with a lady called Monika. Jelisic then started beating up a man. There were about 25 men detained in the room, and then they were shifted to the hotel terrace. They were made to stand in two lines, and Jelisic began to beat two of the men. An older man was thrown amongst the group and was also being beaten. When he complained, he was taken out of the group and shot. A Croat amongst the group was released because he was in the same house as the witness; whereupon, on the basis of being in the same house, the witness and another Muslim were able to secure his release, and he, the witness, was sent to the park. While in the park, the witness was about 50 metres away, and he turned instinctively and saw Jelisic standing there with a handgun and he heard a gunfire burst and saw bodies falling. He was then taken to the SUP building where he was told not to look at anything. He heard five or six more shots. After answering a few questions at the SUP, he was released. A few months later, he was arrested and taken to the Batkovic camp. And, Your Honours, that's the essence of his testimony in his written statement, and we would proffer him for cross-examination at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, at some point when counsel was reading that summary, you appeared to be shaking your head. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there something in that summary that you didn't agree with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: When I saw the bodies -- in that toilet, there is no window there. There is just a door leading to the courtyard where those corpses were lying about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. You've got your -- do you have your statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Can the witness be given his statement, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I've handed him a copy with paragraphs numbered. I have an English version numbered as well, if the Defence counsel would like to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That would be very helpful. I've numbered my own, but I would be interested to see whether they do tally. If Mr. Hannis and I have done what we should have been doing, then they will. Thank you. I'm delighted to say, Your Honour, that Mr. Hannis and I have each done our homework satisfactorily, because right down to the number 29, the numbering matches. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, would you look at paragraph 3, please. Do you see that on the first full page? Do you have that? In English it begins with: "The war in Brcko began with the blowing up of the bridges ..." We're looking at the same page, are we?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There's a tiny error there, because it talks about "over the night of the 31st of April." Well, in that year, as in every other year, there's no such date. You mean the 30th of April to the 1st of May. That's obvious, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: Yes, it must be a typing error.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You then refer to the blowing up of the bridges and then you say: "By the 4th of May, the Serbian offensive was complete and the Serb forces occupied Brcko up to the river, Brka," if that's how it's pronounced. In the summary that Mr. Hannis gave just now, he referred to Serb paramilitaries. You'd agree that here we're talking about Serb paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: I can explain. On the 4th of May, 22 different types of armies entered Brcko. There were paramilitaries, there were volunteers, and there were also the reservists of the JNA. At the same time, the active troops who were in the Brcko garrison had been removed, and they were some 20 kilometres away from the town. And while Brcko was being occupied by all these armies, they were also there. They returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The total number of men at the -- normally at the JNA garrison at Brcko was about 50, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: I don't understand your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The size of the garrison, the number of soldiers who were normally at the JNA garrison at this time in early 1992 was around 50, wasn't it? Or perhaps you don't know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: I have to explain this to you. In the JNA garrison in Brcko where the JNA troops were, officers still remained, and those who had arrived in order to keep peace in town. It is these very people that started making trouble in the town. And then things ensued from that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me. Witness, Witness, I'm going to stop you for the simple reason that you're not answering my question, which is what I wish you to do. Do you know -- not exactly, but do you know roughly -- how many soldiers were normally stationed in the JNA garrison in Brcko in March and April 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: In March and April, there was nobody but officers, the only exception being the month of April when a captain came from the military police and some specials came with him. I wouldn't be able to give you the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So -- well, don't give us the exact number if you can't, then. Can you give the Tribunal the rough number?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ten? Twenty? A hundred? A thousand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: Well, their number changed. Some left; some came. It was very difficult to know how many of them there were at any given time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How long had you lived in Brcko in -- by April 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: From the day I was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what's the population of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: It's mixed population. It's mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... What was the total population in numbers in Brcko in 1992, roughly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: In 1992, the municipality of Brcko had about 43.000 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You see, what I suggest to you, Witness, is that you must have some idea of the rough size or rough numbers stationed in a garrison in the centre of Brcko where you had lived for many years. So tell the Tribunal, please, as best you can, what that rough number was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: The Brcko garrison, up to that period, had about 1.000 soldiers, conscripts, approximately, and maybe there were between 50 and 100 officers. In 1991, the entire garrison was relocated. The soldiers were moved from town, but the kitchen remained which prepared their food, and every day the trucks would -- the food would be taken by trucks to the place where the soldiers were relocated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So from what you're taking, it -- the conclusion seems to be that there was a very small number of men left at the Brcko JNA garrison by April 1992, and according to your evidence, they were only officers. And by a very small number, perhaps I can suggest that it sounds from your evidence as if we're perhaps talking about a couple of dozen or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- I think in witness's testimony he said fifty to a hundred officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but -- I understand from the question, but there seems, then, to be some confusion in that you now asked how many men, not officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's a slightly different confusion, with respect, Your Honours, because his evidence, as I recall it, was that at the time when there were about a thousand soldiers and conscripts there may be between fifty and a hundred officers. That Your Honour, that was -- He was talking about a different time. I'm simply putting to the witness -- it's not my evidence -- a suggestion that he can agree with or disagree with. I'm not saying he has given that specific evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm inviting your agreement, Witness, that the number officers left at the Brcko garrison in April -- sounds from your evidence that it was probably about a couple of a dozen. But if it was more as you remember it, please say so.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: I can say specifically for that period, because I was born there, and I would pass by there on my way to work and on my way back from work, so I'm going back to it again. In 1990, according to my estimate, perhaps there were about 1.000 conscripts there and maybe 50 or 70 officers. In 1991, when the conflict broke out with Croatia, the garrison and the recruits were relocated, and I can even tell you where. They were moved to Pelagicevo Obudovac, which is about 20 kilometres outside of town on the road to Banja Luka. The officers who remained at the garrison, perhaps there were about 20 or 30 of them, I don't know exactly. And the kitchen -- that was the service which was supposed to prepare the meals for the soldiers -- they operated there, and they had the number of staff that they needed in order to work. I didn't enter the compound. I could just look over the fence, through the wire fence. Then with the arrival of the special units, the arrival of the military police, that is now something else, and we could talk about that. We were talking about the recruits of the JNA and the officers who worked with them and who were in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You -- you mentioned that there were 22 different military or paramilitary groups as part of the forces which, according to you, launched some sort of offensive into Brcko in April 1992; correct? Twenty-two was your number. Please -- please --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: Not April.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Correct. Is what I put to you correct or not, as you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: Not in April. This was on the 4th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Early May. Early May. My mistake. End of April, early May. You talk about the 1st of April, first spate of bombing, and then the next few days; correct? So 22 different groups you mention, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to know -- well, first of all, is this number of 22 the result of your logging the different groups that you saw during that period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: Let me give an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, please answer my question first.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you yourself at that time over that actual period, did you yourself make some sort of note or tally or log of the different groups that were entering or launching an offensive in Brcko in early May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So where do you get the number of 22 from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: When we were being taken in, I could see all these various types of uniforms, and I just counted them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You just counted -- so you counted yourself, personally, did you, 22 different types of uniform? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you note them down with pencil and paper as you counted them? I'm sorry, I missed your answer. Or perhaps you didn't give one.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So do you have -- do you have a brain and a memory which without noting down on pieces of paper enables you to tally up in your head different uniforms and come to a specific figure like 22?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: No, I am not so stupid that I don't know how to count.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, no. Witness, please understand, I wouldn't be so offensive to suggest that you can't easily count up to and beyond 22. We're talking about an entirely different exercise, and perhaps I will give you the opportunity to explain a little bit more generally, then. What is process by which you came to this figure of 22?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: Well, I told you, by the uniforms; uniform of the reserve police officer is different from an active police officer. A uniform of an active soldier and a reserve solder is different. A uniform of a member of the special forces and just a person who actually bought the uniform on the street and put it together, they're different. Uniforms of Chetniks with the insignia on them, different insignia are all different. So from my house to the SUP building I saw all these uniforms, and I had the opportunity to count them. The distance we're talking about is some 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The distance from where to where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: From the place where we were assembled to the SUP building where we were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry. So what is -- just explain; what is the significance of the distance of 500 metres in relation to your ability to tally up the 22 different uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: The operation to take over the town began on the day that the bridges were destroyed. That's when various formations began to arrive at the town, and they were accommodated or billeted in the barracks compound and in other places. On the 4th of May, the main offensive was launched to take over the town, and from all sides they came in, from the side of Bijeljina; actually from all sides, except the side which is across from the Brka river and leads to Banja Luka. They captured the town on the 4th of May, and then they stopped because --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... We will come to this, perhaps, but at the moment that does not appear to be at all directly an answer to the question I asked, so may I come back to that. Would you now be able to reconstitute, if you thought hard about it, would you be able to reconstitute your list of 22 different uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: I just gave you a few examples of uniforms, what they looked like and what the people looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: My question was whether you would now, if you had a bit of time, would you be able to reconstitute, draw up again your list of 22 -- it was a mental list, of course, according to you -- but would you be able to list those 22 uniforms if you were given a little time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: Well, I can explain it to you, and I can tell I right away. Again --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I'm asking you at the moment, please, it would be very helpful, Witness, in the first place answer as directly as possible the specific question I ask. Is it yes or no: Would you be able, if you were given a little time, to draw up again now that list of 22 uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018
utterances.text: I could do that, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Right. Good. In that case witness may I suggest --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say that I do have one very brief matter, nothing to do with the evidence, that I would like the opportunity of raising in about two minutes. So if I were to invite the witness to, over the -- we have an adjournment now until Tuesday, we have a long weekend. If I were to invite the witness to do that exercise, between now and Tuesday, so I can pursue that line of cross-examination when the Tribunal reconvenes on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Usually, Mr. Stewart, if we ask the witness to do something out of court, it is usual that the Chamber asks the witness to use this kind of exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, may I through the Tribunal invite the witness to do that exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please write down the 22 different types of military men or uniforms, the list of 22 you spoke about, could you write them down over the weekend and perhaps then present it to the Chamber when your cross-examination will continue. Would you be willing to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. No problem. I can do that. I can also explain it orally what each one of them looked like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, then perhaps we leave that to Mr. Stewart, whether he would seek any further explanation on that. And the Chamber, of course, will also look at your list. But you're invited to do that over the weekend. Is there another issue, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There is. It neither concerns the witness, but nor would it be at all embarrassing for the witness to be sitting there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I say, Your Honour, there was no discourtesy intended and my invitation was the way I am familiar with doing it. But I now understand the correct courtesy and that's the way I will channel my requests in future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mainly for outside court activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, for outside. I shan't ask permission for every question, Your Honour. That would slow things down. May I also add this: I'm sure that -- well, I'm confident the Tribunal will endorse this -- if it could be made clear to the witness that in drawing up this list he is to consult nobody else. He is to do it himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I always instruct witnesses at the end when they leave the courtroom when we adjourn not to consult.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I know Your Honour does. I was thinking specifically of this task, with the temptation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the point I wish to raise is only this, and it arose earlier on. It has to do with the public nature of the proceedings, because Your Honour -- and we on the Defence side endorse this 100 per cent -- Your Honour and the Chamber were adamant that, if at all possible, the Court should sit if public session and not private session, and at the 65 ter meeting that was emphasised. We adhere to that and endorse it 100 per cent. Although we understand the practical reasons why often if, for example, in a previous case evidence was given in private session, at least that raises the distinct possibility that it might be appropriate to continue, Your Honour could we say that we don't -- we submit that it doesn't follow automatically. It doesn't. It shouldn't justify an enormous review. But, Your Honour, we would -- on the Defence side -- Mr. Krajisnik on these charges is, as I'm sure Your Honour will accept 100 per cent, entitled to the most public trial that is possible. So we do invite the Tribunal and this will be the Defence's position, that any question of going into private session at any point must have a specific justification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Only the other hand, you know that the Rules provide for automatic extension of protective measures in other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course. In relation to protective measures we understand that completely, Your Honour. That's part of the mechanism, and we don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let me just be short. From the mere fact that you convinced us or that we convinced ourselves that we should first look in the transcript of the testimony and see whether it could do any harm, we took that effort in order to not unnecessarily go into private session on an issue where it would not directly follow from the protective measures in effect. And I think that's the approach you can expect from the Chamber, generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm much obliged, Your Honour. There doesn't seem to be anything between us on that matter. I have nothing more to add this evening, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Anything else more to be raised before the weekend, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, it's Friday evening, 7.00. We'll adjourn for the weekend, but since this Chamber will not sit next Monday, you're expected to come back on Tuesday, next today at 9.00 in the morning, not the same courtroom, but you'll certainly be guided to Courtroom II, where we will sit. You are instructed not to speak to anybody about your testimony -- nor outsiders, nor parties -- and I specifically ask you, when you're making that list of 22, not to consult anyone but just to do it on your own memory. We will adjourn until Tuesday, the 10th of February, 9.00, Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 10th day of February, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.03 p.m.
